Section 4.1 — The Home as the First Proof of Ministry

We ended the last unit with a promise to take up the pastor's family, and we do so now because Scripture itself places the home at the very center of a man's fitness for the office. It is easy to imagine that a pastor's home is the private backdrop to his public work — the place he retreats to after the real ministry is done. The Bible turns that picture exactly around. The home is not the backdrop to the ministry; it is the first proving ground of it.

Paul makes the logic inescapable. Among the qualifications for an overseer, he writes that a man must be "one who rules his own house well, having his children in submission with all reverence" — and then he presses the reason home with a question that has no comfortable answer: "for if a man does not know how to rule his own house, how will he take care of the church of God?" (1 Timothy 3:4–5). Read that as the argument it is. The household is the smaller trust by which God tests a man's fitness for the larger one. A man who cannot shepherd the few souls placed under his own roof, who cannot lead with love and patience the wife and children who know him best, has given no evidence that he can shepherd the many. The church is, in a real sense, simply the household of God writ large, and the qualifying test runs from the small house to the great one.

This means that the order of a pastor's priorities is settled before he ever sets it himself. His walk with God comes first, as we saw in Unit 3; his family comes next; and the church, for all its weight, comes after the family it must never be allowed to consume. The home is also a witness, and not only a test. The watching world and the watching congregation read a pastor's doctrine of grace, of patience, of love, far more clearly in how he treats his wife at the end of a hard week than in his most polished sermon on the subject. What he is at home is what he actually believes. The rest is theory.
Section 4.2 — The Husband’s Loving Leadership and the Father’s Charge

Scripture assigns the husband a position of leadership in the home, and we will not apologize for teaching it, because God's Word teaches it. But everything turns on how that leadership is defined, and here the Bible's definition is so far from the world's caricature that the two can scarcely be spoken of in the same breath. The world hears "headship" and imagines domination, the strong imposing his will on the weak. Paul hears it and points to a cross. "Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the church and gave Himself for her" (Ephesians 5:25). There is the pattern, and it is devastating to every form of petty male tyranny. The head of the home is to lead the way Christ led — by laying himself down, by serving, by spending himself for the good of the one entrusted to him, even unto death. A husband's authority is real, but it is the authority of the one who washes feet. The man who uses headship as a license for selfishness has not understood the first thing about it; he has inverted it.

The same self-giving love reaches down to the children. "And you, fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath, but bring them up in the training and admonition of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). Notice that the charge cuts in two directions at once. There is a positive duty — to bring them up, to train, to instruct, to point them again and again to the Lord. And there is a sharp negative warning — do not provoke them, do not exasperate them with harshness, inconsistency, or a standard you demand of them but never of yourself. A great many children raised in the manse have been driven not toward Christ but away from Him, not by the gospel their father preached but by the bitterness their father bred at home. Parenting in a pastor's house must hold these together: a discipline that is firm but never cruel, and a tenderness that is warm but never indulgent, all of it aimed at the heart and not merely the behavior.
Section 4.3 — Purity, Singleness, and the Question of Divorce and Remarriage

Sexual purity is required of every servant of God, the married no less than the single, and we will treat its hardest modern pressures in a later unit. Here we lay the foundation. The married man guards his purity by cherishing his own wife and by fleeing, as Joseph fled, every situation that would compromise him. The single man — and let us say plainly that singleness is no second-class calling; our Lord Himself was single, and the apostle Paul commended it as a gift — guards his purity by chastity and by the same fleeing. The standard is one heart, kept clean before God, whatever a man's marital state.

This brings us to marriage's permanence, and to one of the most pastorally difficult questions a minister will ever face. Scripture holds an exceedingly high view of the marriage covenant. It is not a contract to be dissolved when it ceases to please, but a covenant joined by God: "Therefore what God has joined together, let not man separate" (Matthew 19:6). The biblical default, the thing we must teach and model, is permanence. Within that high view, the New Testament names certain grounds on which a marriage may be biblically dissolved — our Lord's words concerning sexual immorality (Matthew 19:9), and Paul's concerning desertion by an unbelieving spouse (1 Corinthians 7:15). I will tell you honestly that faithful, conservative, Bible-believing men have differed over exactly how far these exceptions extend and whether they permit remarriage, and a wise pastor holds his convictions here firmly while granting that godly brothers land in somewhat different places. What no faithful pastor may do is either to cheapen the covenant by treating divorce as easy, or to crush the wounded by treating the divorced as though they were beyond the reach of grace. The same gospel that upholds the permanence of marriage also binds up those whose marriages have broken, and the pastor must be a faithful guardian of the first without ever becoming a hard man toward the second.
Section 4.4 — Protecting the Family from the Pressures of Ministry

There is a peculiar set of pressures that falls on a pastor's family and on no other, and the man who does not see them coming will let them do their quiet damage unopposed. The first is the fishbowl. The pastor's wife and children live their lives under a scrutiny no one elected them to bear, watched and judged by a congregation that often expects of them a perfection it does not expect of itself. A wise pastor shields his family from that glare, refuses to make his children into sermon illustrations, and never lets the church's expectations be laid as a yoke on shoulders too small to carry them.

The second and graver pressure is subtler, and I have watched it destroy more ministers' homes than any scandal. It is the slow theft of the man from his own family by the very work he loves. The ministry is endless; there is always one more visit, one more meeting, one more soul in need, and a conscientious pastor can always find holy-sounding reasons to give the church the time and the best energies that belonged to his wife and children. The church becomes, in effect, a mistress — not of the body, but of the heart and the hours — and the family is left with a husband and father who is present in the house but absent from the home. Do not do this. Guard your days. Defend the evening, the table, the Sabbath rest, the ordinary unhurried time in which a marriage and a family are actually built. Learn to say no to good things in order to protect the best things.

For let us be perfectly clear about what is at stake. It will profit a man nothing to gain the whole church and lose his own children. The man who builds a thriving ministry on the rubble of his neglected family has not succeeded; he has committed a tragedy with a respectable face. The faithful pastor finishes his course, as we said, having kept the faith — and he keeps it first of all in the small, holy congregation that bears his own name. Tend that flock well, and you will be the better shepherd of the larger one. Neglect it, and no measure of public success will ever make up the loss.

sa.prompt: 21. Why does the unit call the pastor's home the first proving ground of his ministry, using 1 Timothy 3?
sa.model: 1 Timothy 3:4-5 asks that if a man cannot rule his own house, how will he take care of the church of God. The home is not the private backdrop to real ministry but its first proving ground. The household is the smaller trust by which God tests a man's fitness for the larger trust of the church, which is simply the household of God writ large. A man's life at home is therefore the first evidence of his fitness for office.

es_reference.prompt: 21. ¿Por qué llama la unidad al hogar del pastor el primer campo de prueba de su ministerio, usando 1 Timoteo 3?
es_reference.model: 1 Timoteo 3:4-5 pregunta que si un hombre no puede gobernar su propia casa, cómo cuidará de la iglesia de Dios. El hogar no es el telón de fondo privado del ministerio real sino su primer campo de prueba. El hogar es la confianza menor por la cual Dios prueba la idoneidad de un hombre para la confianza mayor de la iglesia, que es sencillamente la casa de Dios en grande. La vida de un hombre en casa es por tanto la primera evidencia de su idoneidad para el oficio.

sa.prompt: 22. State the settled order of a pastor's priorities and why the church must never consume the family.
sa.model: The settled order is a pastor's walk with God first, then his family, then the church, which for all its weight comes after the family it must never be allowed to consume. The reason is that the home is the first proving ground of the ministry and also a witness: a man's real doctrine of grace, patience, and love is read most clearly in how he treats his wife at the end of a hard week, far more than in his most polished sermon. What he is at home is what he actually believes. And it will profit a man nothing to gain the whole church and lose his own children.

es_reference.prompt: 22. Exponga el orden establecido de las prioridades de un pastor y por qué la iglesia nunca debe consumir a la familia.
es_reference.model: El orden establecido es primero el andar del pastor con Dios, luego su familia, y después la iglesia, que, por mucho que pese, viene después de la familia a la que nunca debe permitirse devorar. La razón es que el hogar es el primer campo de prueba del ministerio y también un testimonio: la verdadera doctrina de gracia, paciencia y amor de un hombre se lee con más claridad en cómo trata a su esposa al final de una semana difícil que en su sermón más pulido. Lo que es en casa es lo que realmente cree. Y de nada le sirve a un hombre ganar toda la iglesia y perder a sus propios hijos.

sa.prompt: 23. How does the unit redefine 'headship,' and what does Ephesians 5:25 require of husbands?
sa.model: When the world hears 'headship' it imagines domination, but when Paul speaks of it he points not to a throne but to a cross. Ephesians 5:25 commands husbands to love their wives just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her. A husband's authority is real but is the authority of the one who washes feet, exercised in self-giving love rather than command. Headship is cruciform, not domineering.

es_reference.prompt: 23. ¿Cómo redefine la unidad la «jefatura», y qué exige Efesios 5:25 de los maridos?
es_reference.model: Cuando el mundo oye «jefatura» imagina dominación, pero cuando Pablo habla de ella señala no un trono sino una cruz. Efesios 5:25 manda a los maridos amar a sus esposas así como Cristo amó a la iglesia y se entregó a sí mismo por ella. La autoridad de un esposo es real pero es la autoridad del que lava los pies, ejercida en amor que se entrega y no en mando. La jefatura tiene forma de cruz, no de dominación.

sa.prompt: 24. What does Ephesians 6:4 charge fathers to do and not do, and what warning does the unit add?
sa.model: Ephesians 6:4 charges fathers not to provoke their children to wrath, and positively to bring them up in the training and admonition of the Lord. The charge cuts in two directions: there is a positive duty to bring them up, to train, to instruct, to point them again and again to the Lord, and a sharp negative warning not to exasperate them with harshness, inconsistency, or a standard demanded of them but never of oneself. The unit warns soberly that a great many children raised in the manse have been driven not toward Christ but away from Him, not by the gospel their father preached but by the bitterness their father bred at home. Parenting in a pastor's house must hold the two together: a discipline that is firm but never cruel, and a tenderness that is warm but never indulgent, all of it aimed at the heart and not merely the behavior.

es_reference.prompt: 24. ¿Qué encarga Efesios 6:4 a los padres hacer y no hacer, y qué advertencia añade la unidad?
es_reference.model: Efesios 6:4 manda a los padres no provocar a ira a sus hijos y, positivamente, criarlos en la disciplina y amonestación del Señor. El mandato corta en dos direcciones: hay un deber positivo de criarlos, formarlos, instruirlos y apuntarlos una y otra vez al Señor, y una advertencia negativa tajante de no exasperarlos con dureza, inconsistencia o una norma que se les exige a ellos pero nunca a uno mismo. La unidad advierte con seriedad que muchísimos hijos criados en la casa pastoral han sido llevados no hacia Cristo sino lejos de Él, no por el evangelio que predicó su padre sino por la amargura que su padre crió en casa. La crianza en la casa de un pastor debe sostener ambas cosas: una disciplina firme pero nunca cruel y una ternura cálida pero nunca indulgente, todo dirigido al corazón y no solo a la conducta.

sa.prompt: 25. Summarize the unit's teaching on the permanence of marriage and the pastor's two opposite errors.
sa.model: Marriage is not a contract to be dissolved at will but a covenant joined by God; 'what God has joined together, let not man separate' sets the biblical default of permanence. The New Testament names sexual immorality and desertion by an unbelieving spouse among the grounds discussed, and faithful conservative men have differed over how far the exceptions extend. The pastor must avoid two opposite errors: cheapening the covenant on one hand, and crushing the divorced as beyond grace on the other.

es_reference.prompt: 25. Resuma la enseñanza de la unidad sobre la permanencia del matrimonio y los dos errores opuestos del pastor.
es_reference.model: El matrimonio no es un contrato para disolverse a voluntad sino un pacto unido por Dios; «lo que Dios juntó, no lo separe el hombre» fija el valor bíblico por defecto de la permanencia. El Nuevo Testamento nombra la inmoralidad sexual y el abandono por un cónyuge incrédulo entre los fundamentos tratados, y hombres fieles y conservadores han diferido sobre cuán lejos se extienden las excepciones. El pastor debe evitar dos errores opuestos: abaratar el pacto por un lado, y aplastar a los divorciados como fuera de la gracia por el otro.

sa.prompt: 26. Why is singleness no second-class calling, and of whom is purity required?
sa.model: The unit states plainly that singleness is no second-class calling. Sexual purity is required of the married no less than the single. The married man guards his purity by cherishing his wife and fleeing temptation as Joseph fled, and the single man by the same vigilance. Purity is a universal call, not a burden laid only on one station of life.

es_reference.prompt: 26. ¿Por qué la soltería no es un llamamiento de segunda clase, y de quién se exige la pureza?
es_reference.model: La unidad afirma con claridad que la soltería no es un llamamiento de segunda clase. La pureza sexual se exige del casado no menos que del soltero. El hombre casado guarda su pureza apreciando a su esposa y huyendo de la tentación como huyó José, y el soltero por la misma vigilancia. La pureza es un llamado universal, no una carga puesta solo sobre un estado de la vida.

sa.prompt: 27. Describe the two peculiar pressures the unit warns press on a pastor's family.
sa.model: The first pressure is the fishbowl of constant scrutiny; a wise pastor shields his family from the glare, refusing for instance to make his children into sermon illustrations. The graver, subtler pressure is the slow theft of the man from his family by the very work he loves, until the all-consuming church becomes a mistress of the heart and the hours. Both must be named and actively resisted.

es_reference.prompt: 27. Describa las dos presiones peculiares que la unidad advierte que pesan sobre la familia de un pastor.
es_reference.model: La primera presión es la pecera del escrutinio constante; un pastor sabio protege a su familia del resplandor, rehusando por ejemplo convertir a sus hijos en ilustraciones de sermón. La más grave y sutil es el lento robo del hombre a su familia por la obra misma que ama, hasta que la iglesia que todo lo consume se vuelve una amante del corazón y de las horas. Ambas deben ser nombradas y resistidas activamente.

sa.prompt: 28. Explain the warning that a thriving ministry can be 'a tragedy with a respectable face.'
sa.model: It will profit a man nothing to gain the whole church and lose his own children. A thriving ministry built on a neglected family is a tragedy with a respectable face—admired publicly while quietly ruinous at home. To prevent it the pastor must guard his days and learn to say no to good things in order to protect the best things. The applause of the larger flock is no compensation for the small congregation that bears his own name.

es_reference.prompt: 28. Explique la advertencia de que un ministerio floreciente puede ser «una tragedia con rostro respetable».
es_reference.model: De nada le aprovechará a un hombre ganar toda la iglesia y perder a sus propios hijos. Un ministerio floreciente edificado sobre una familia descuidada es una tragedia con rostro respetable — admirado en público mientras es silenciosamente ruinoso en casa. Para impedirlo el pastor debe guardar sus días y aprender a decir no a cosas buenas para proteger las mejores. El aplauso de la grey mayor no compensa la pequeña congregación que lleva su propio nombre.

sa.prompt: 29. How does tending one's own family well relate to shepherding the larger flock?
sa.model: The faithful pastor keeps the faith first of all in the small congregation that bears his own name. Far from competing with his ministry, tending his own family well makes him the better shepherd of the larger flock, because the home is where his character is proved and displayed. The pastor's family is both a test of his fitness and a witness to what he truly believes.

es_reference.prompt: 29. ¿Cómo se relaciona cuidar bien la propia familia con pastorear la grey mayor?
es_reference.model: El pastor fiel guarda la fe ante todo en la pequeña congregación que lleva su propio nombre. Lejos de competir con su ministerio, cuidar bien su propia familia lo hace el mejor pastor de la grey mayor, porque el hogar es donde su carácter se prueba y se exhibe. La familia del pastor es a la vez una prueba de su idoneidad y un testimonio de lo que de veras cree.

sa.prompt: 30. Why is the pastor's family both a test of fitness and a witness to his belief?
sa.model: The family is a test of fitness because the smaller trust of the household reveals whether a man can be entrusted with the larger trust of the church. It is a witness because a man's real convictions about grace, love, and authority are displayed at home more honestly than anywhere else. What a congregation watches a pastor be at home shapes them more than his finest sermon. So the home both qualifies the man and preaches his true belief.

es_reference.prompt: 30. ¿Por qué es la familia del pastor a la vez una prueba de idoneidad y un testimonio de su creencia?
es_reference.model: La familia es una prueba de idoneidad porque la confianza menor del hogar revela si un hombre puede ser confiado con la confianza mayor de la iglesia. Es un testimonio porque las verdaderas convicciones de un hombre acerca de la gracia, el amor y la autoridad se exhiben en casa más honestamente que en cualquier otro lugar. Lo que una congregación observa que un pastor es en casa la moldea más que su mejor sermón. Así el hogar a la vez califica al hombre y predica su verdadera creencia.
